details: Symptoms group into four clusters: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance of reminders, negative changes in mood and thinking, and hyperarousal (startle, scanning, poor sleep).
A reaction in the first days after a call is an acute stress reaction. PTSD is the pattern that persists — the diagnosis needs symptoms lasting more than a month.
On scene, a patient whose old trauma is re-triggered may startle, pull away, or shut down. That is a brain state, not non-compliance: calm voice, warn before touch, no sudden moves.
Federal monitoring of 9/11 responders found roughly 1 in 5 developed PTSD. Responder exposure is cumulative, which is why departments track it like an injury.
posttraumatic stress disorder.economics: Many states have passed presumption laws: a first responder's PTSD is presumed to be work-related for workers' compensation. That shifts the cost of treatment to the employer and insurer, instead of the responder having to prove which single call caused it.
posttraumatic stress disorder.history: The pattern is old; the name is new. Civil War doctors wrote of 'soldier's heart'; the World Wars called it shell shock and combat fatigue, and it was often treated as weakness. Vietnam veterans' advocacy pushed it into the DSM-III in 1980 as post-traumatic stress disorder — the first time the diagnosis named the event, not the person, as the cause. That shift turned it from a character verdict into a treatable injury.
posttraumatic stress disorder.science: Three structures run the pattern. The amygdala is the threat detector — in PTSD it is hyperreactive, firing on cues that resemble the trauma (a tone pitch, a smell, a street). The hippocampus normally stamps a memory with its time and place ('that was then, this is now'); in PTSD it underworks, so a memory arrives without its time stamp and a flashback feels present, not past. The medial prefrontal cortex is the brake that appraises the alarm and calms it — in PTSD it under-fires, so the alarm runs unchecked. The chemistry: norepinephrine stays elevated (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, broken sleep), while cortisol is often LOW, not high — the HPA loop (hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal glands) over-corrected after chronic activation. The common guess, 'stress hormones are just high,' catches only half the system.
posttraumatic stress disorder.what: PTSD is a lasting stress disorder after a traumatic event: the alarm system keeps firing as if the event were still happening — intrusive memories and nightmares, avoidance, negative mood, and hyperarousal that do not settle with time.

details: The Exposure Control Plan is the employer's written plan, required by OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030. It lists which jobs and tasks expose workers, how exposure is reduced, and how an exposure incident gets evaluated.
OSHA requires the plan to be reviewed and updated at least once a year, and kept where employees can read it.

The employer must offer the hepatitis B vaccine free, within 10 working days of assignment to work with exposure risk. Declining takes a signed declination form, and the offer stands if the worker changes his mind later.
After any exposure: wash right away, report it, and get a medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee. The evaluation is confidential.

Owners, kept straight: OSHA writes what employers must do to protect workers. NHTSA writes what EMTs are taught (the National EMS Education Standards and the Scope of Practice Model). Different owners, different books.
bloodborne pathogens.economics: The vaccine series, the post-exposure evaluation, and the follow-up are all paid by the employer, not the EMT — the standard puts the cost on the party who controls the workplace. Safer sharps devices cost more per unit; the 2000 Act made employers buy them anyway, because one needlestick's testing, treatment, follow-up, and lost work cost far more.
bloodborne pathogens.history: OSHA published the Bloodborne Pathogens standard in December 1991, in the middle of the AIDS crisis, after years of health care workers being infected on the job with no federal rule requiring protection. The Ryan White CARE Act (1990) had already created the designated-officer notification system for responders exposed to a patient. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act (2000) then forced safer sharps and a sharps injury log into the standard (updated January 2001). Ryan White's own story is the era in one life: a boy with hemophilia, infected at 13 by pooled factor VIII concentrate in 1984, before the blood supply was screened.
bloodborne pathogens.science: Three hazards ride in blood, and they live in different places. Hepatitis B and hepatitis C attack the liver (hepatocytes) and circulate in the blood; hepatitis B also reaches semen, vaginal fluids, and saliva, so it spreads by more routes. HIV attacks the immune system itself — the CD4 helper T cells — copying itself inside them and destroying them; as the CD4 count falls below 200, the stage is AIDS. One-line contrast: Hep B and Hep C live in the liver and ride the blood out; HIV lives in the immune cells that ride in the blood. Hep B has a vaccine, Hep C now has a cure (8 to 12 weeks of antivirals for most people), HIV has neither — treatment suppresses it. Per needlestick from an infected patient, hepatitis B infects an unvaccinated person up to roughly 1 time in 3; hepatitis C about 2 in 100; HIV about 3 in 1,000 — which is why hepatitis B discipline comes first.
bloodborne pathogens.what: Bloodborne pathogens are viruses and bacteria carried in human blood (and some other body fluids) that can infect a provider through a break in the skin, a needlestick, or a splash to the eyes, nose, or mouth.
